Data Science for Finance · Fall 2026 · Albert Aldrich and William Harkless

Can an agent that only sees rewards find a near-optimal portfolio?

Nine ETFs, a simulator calibrated once, a Q-learning agent choosing among 1,287 long-only portfolios.

Part I · data and calibration

The environment: 20 years of daily data, estimated once and frozen

  • SPY, EFA, EEM · IEF, LQD, TIP · GLD, VNQ, DBC
  • Adjusted Close, simple excess returns, one daily frequency
  • 7 Feb 2006 to 31 Jul 2026, inner-joined, nothing imputed
  • Gaussian simulator with μ and Σ fixed; the agent sees simulated rewards only

Part II · theory

Two benchmarks under the agent's own constraints

530.5
bps/yr: value of the long-only optimum at γ = 5
5.7
bps/yr discretization gap on the 20% grid (11.7 at 25%, 1.3 at 10%)
3 of 9
ETFs held by the optimum: SPY, IEF, GLD

U(w) = w′μ − (γ/2)·w′Σw, long-only and fully invested for theory and agent alike. The grid is built from the asset count and the step only; the optimum is never inserted.

3
Part III · design

The agent: one value per portfolio, updated with averaged rewards

  • Stateless, 1,287 actions (20% grid)
  • Reward: 20-day realized mean − (γ/2) × realized variance, so E[reward] = U(w)
  • Update: Q(a) ← Q(a) + (1/N(a))·[R − Q(a)], discount 0
  • ε-greedy, ε = e−βt, 1% at the halfway episode
  • Settings and convergence rule fixed before any full-scale run

Bonus extension 1 · a negative result on the 10% grid

Spline function approximation: better ranking, worse top pick on the large grid

43.5 → 15.7
20% grid, γ = 5: constant-α table vs splines (baseline 17.6)
11.7 → 78.8
10% grid, γ = 5: 1/N table vs constant-α splines (paired +67.1, SE 9.1)
0.976 vs 0.543
Spearman on the 10% grid at γ = 5, splines vs table; at the median splines find none of the true top ten

No constant-α table was run on the 10% grid, so that comparison also changes the step rule; on the 20% grid the constant step alone costs the table 25.9 bps/yr at γ = 5. Step sizes were tuned by scoring final portfolios on simulated draws.

The agent's gap to the oracle narrows as costs rise, from 13.1 bps/yr to 2.8

Most of the narrowing at $10B comes from a target closer to the best one, which we have not explained. There the agent is statistically indistinguishable from the myopic policy, which knows μ, Σ and the costs (−0.5, SE 0.54).

12

Conclusions

What it learned

The right assets and a near-optimal mix, from rewards alone. It follows the optimum toward bonds as γ rises.

14.1 / 19.8
bps/yr from the best grid portfolio / the optimum (median, γ = 5)

What stopped it

Reward noise about 370 times the difference between the top two portfolios. Finer grids and richer models move the error around at this budget.

3 of 10
seeds exactly right at γ = 5; 5 of 10 at γ = 3 and 8

What it rests on

A stationary Gaussian world, μ and Σ taken as true, 260M simulated days per seed. Only the four baseline experiments were pre-registered.

310.9
bps/yr lost by equal weight, for scale

Post hoc: the 10% grid, the episode-length, budget and exploration variants, function approximation, transaction costs. Benchmark information entered design choices (episode budget; the transaction-cost universe, cost levels and features) and never reached the agent.
